These are the ballot-measure sections of the guide I circulated for the November 2026 election. Recommendations reflect my views at that time. They are not election results or verified implementation findings. The original circulation date has not been established.

The candidate commentary from the supplied guide is outside this archive’s ballot-measure scope. Original ballot explanations and reasoning are retained below; formatting has been normalized. ## Question 1 — Funding state employee labor agreements {#question-1}

{{< include ../_ballot_text/md-1.qmd >}}

Overview: Requires the governor’s proposed budget to include funding for state employee collective bargaining agreements, including terms decided by a neutral arbitrator. It governs the proposed budget, not the final appropriation.

- Pro: Makes negotiated wages and benefits more meaningful and strengthens workers’ bargaining position.  
- Con: Reduces executive budget flexibility when labor costs compete with other public-service needs.

**Vote: YES** — Always for additional workers' rights/influence.

## Question 2 — Temporary members for judicial oversight {#question-2}

{{< include ../_ballot_text/md-2.qmd >}}

Overview: Allows temporary replacements on the Commission on Judicial Disabilities when members are recused, disqualified, or finish their terms without replacements. Substitutes must meet constitutional eligibility requirements.

- Pro: Helps keep judicial accountability proceedings moving despite vacancies or conflicts of interest.  
- Con: Gives the commission chair and governor additional discretion over temporary membership; transparency around selections matters.

**Vote: YES** — I support keeping judicial oversight functioning.

## Question 3 — Congressional redistricting rules {#question-3}

{{< include ../_ballot_text/md-3.qmd >}}

Overview: Removes Maryland constitutional criteria governing congressional district boundaries while retaining state legislative district standards. Also lets lawmakers authorize direct review of congressional maps by Maryland’s highest court. Federal requirements still apply.

- Pro: From a partisan-strategy perspective, gives Maryland’s Democratic majority more flexibility to counter Republican gerrymandering elsewhere.  
- Con: From a democracy-reform perspective, weakens state safeguards against gerrymandering and makes it easier for the governing party to entrench itself. This is not an independent-redistricting reform.

**Vote: NO** — I understand the fight but I just don't believe in gerrymandering even if it's my side doing it.

## Question A — Affordable housing {#question-a}

{{< include ../_ballot_text/baltimore-a.qmd >}}

Overview: Authorizes up to $22 million for affordable housing, rehabilitation, homeownership assistance, related improvements, and other eligible housing uses.

- Pro: Supports housing stability and affordable rental and ownership opportunities.  
- Con: Broad spending authority makes affordability terms, displacement protections, and recipient oversight important.

**Vote: YES** — with the information presented I am guessing this is going to be used as a neighborhood stabilization program.

## Question B — Schools {#question-b}

{{< include ../_ballot_text/baltimore-b.qmd >}}

Overview: Authorizes up to $60 million for school buildings, equipment, athletic facilities, and related community health and recreation facilities.

- Pro: Invests in public education and better learning environments.  
- Con: Borrowing requires repayment; equitable project selection matters. This is not a dedicated teacher-pay or classroom-staffing measure.

**Vote: LEAN YES** — Obviously I am all for school funding but I really do wonder how insulated this will or won't be from the impending drop in enrollment.

## Question C — Community and economic development {#question-c}

{{< include ../_ballot_text/baltimore-c.qmd >}}

Overview: Authorizes up to $50 million for neighborhood revitalization, blight reduction, business assistance, housing improvements, and related development.

- Pro: Can support neglected neighborhoods, home repairs, local businesses, and jobs.  
- Con: Broad eligibility also permits commercial subsidies; benefits could favor developers or accelerate displacement without safeguards.

**Vote: YES** — In addition to the 22 million above this looks like some deliberate development across the whole city.

## Question D — Public infrastructure {#question-d}

{{< include ../_ballot_text/baltimore-d.qmd >}}

Overview: Authorizes up to $148 million for city facilities, libraries, parks, streets, utilities, technology, trees, and related infrastructure.

- Pro: Supports public assets and services residents depend on.  
- Con: Broad authorization does not itself guarantee priority for underserved neighborhoods or environmentally beneficial projects.

**Vote: YES** — I love this kind of spending. Seems high with the last 72 million so I am going to have to dig into the overall direction of this investment.

## Question E — Contract bidding and awards {#question-e}

{{< include ../_ballot_text/baltimore-e.qmd >}}

Overview: Removes charter requirements covering lowest-bid awards, tied bids, and certain contractor bonds, allowing these subjects to be governed through other rules. Removed provisions take effect by November 2028 unless replaced sooner.

- Pro: Could allow purchasing decisions to weigh quality and long-term value rather than price alone.  
- Con: Removes existing guardrails without itself guaranteeing strong replacement standards for transparency, fair competition, or labor protections.

**Vote: YES** — Lowest bid mandates often fail at reducing costs. They keep a lot of potential contractors, especially minority owned firms from being able to beat the larger more established firms.

## Question F — Budget process and Board of Estimates {#question-f}

{{< include ../_ballot_text/baltimore-f.qmd >}}

Overview: Transfers numerous budget and financial responsibilities from the Board of Estimates to the mayor, Finance Department, or Planning Commission; changes veto deadlines; eliminates the preliminary budget hearing process; and removes the $1 million cap on the emergency contingency fund. Some other responsibilities could be reassigned by ordinance.

- Pro: Could clarify responsibility and reduce procedural bottlenecks by placing financial functions with designated officials and departments.  
- Con: Raises public-participation and checks-and-balances concerns: fewer preliminary hearing requirements, more executive responsibility, and removal of the existing charter cap on the contingency fund.

**Vote: NO** — this would reduce oversight by granting more executive authority.

## Question G — Franchises and minor privileges {#question-g}

{{< include ../_ballot_text/baltimore-g.qmd >}}

Overview: Protects the stormwater system from sale or franchise rental, clarifies that conduit space—but not the conduit system itself—may be rented as a franchise, and shifts certain permissions for uses of city property to an executive-agency process established by ordinance.

- Pro: Adds an explicit public-ownership protection for stormwater infrastructure and may simplify routine permissions.  
- Con: Moves some decisions away from the Board of Estimates; replacement procedures will determine how much public scrutiny and accountability remain.

**Vote: YES** — Public infrastructure should be owned by the public, and this adds protection for the stormwater system. What’s murky is how they will rent conduit space, but who knew this was even a thing previously.

## Question H — Separate water and wastewater department {#question-h}

{{< include ../_ballot_text/baltimore-h.qmd >}}

Overview: Creates a Department of Water and Wastewater, transferring these functions out of Public Works beginning January 2029. Also removes the charter requirement that Public Works bureaus be created or abolished by ordinance.

- Pro: Dedicated leadership could give essential water services clearer responsibility and attention.  
- Con: Reorganization alone does not guarantee affordable bills or better service; removing the ordinance requirement reduces a formal council role in Public Works restructuring.

**Vote: LEAN NO** — This is an interesting one. While it may increase efficiency it certainly increases bureaucracy which I don't care for and lessens Council control over DPW which I read as concentrating power elsewhere which only leaves more executive power or unelected bureaucrats.

## Question I — Baltimore Baby Fund {#question-i}

{{< include ../_ballot_text/baltimore-i.qmd >}}

Overview: Creates a protected fund for families with newborns, with an annual city contribution equivalent to 3 cents per $100 of taxable property value. Uses existing property-tax revenue rather than automatically increasing the tax rate. Funds cannot replace existing newborn funding or be transferred to unrelated purposes.

- Pro: Creates sustained, protected investment in families at a financially vulnerable stage, with potential to reduce economic inequality.  
- Con: Earmarks revenue that could otherwise support other needs. The amendment does not itself specify each family’s payment, eligibility rules, or the precise program design.

**Vote: LEAN YES** — I can't possibly be against this as I believe baby bonds, UBI, and similar universal social safety net programs are going to be required as we continue to progress in the age of AI, late stage capitalism, and other forces but this item leaves a lot to question.
